content.thinking:
I'm planning out the whole module in one pass, designing a slender elf ranger character around 1.85m tall with anime proportions, laying out the skeleton structure from hips through spine, neck, and head.

I'm working out the rest pose with arms slightly extended outward and the bow held vertically in the left hand, calculating exact coordinates so the bow's lower tip clears the floor. I'm being careful to track every imported name so nothing goes unused, since I can't test this and need the types to check out on the first try, and I'm mapping out height proportions using a 7.5-head-tall anime ratio with hips at 0.98m, shoulders near 1.5m, and head center around 1.7m.

Now I'm building the skeleton hierarchy, starting with a hips root joint and defining a spine chain through catmull-rom points rising from the hips to the chest, assigning joint names to each span and making sure the chain's parent and starting position align correctly with the hips joint.

Then I'm adding a neck chain branching off the top spine joint through two more points up to the base of the head, followed by a head joint placed near the top of the neck with direction vectors defining its orientation, preferring named local axes like forward/up over raw numeric directions for robustness.

I'll switch to defining everything in absolute model coordinates and assign bones explicitly rather than relying on hierarchy for placement. Setting up the head bone and jaw joint positions, then shaping the skull and chin using small ellipsoid/sphere primitives with specific radii and offsets to sketch the anime-style face.

Now I'm placing the eyes as decals projected onto the skull surface, computing their x-offset and projection direction so they land symmetrically near the top of the face, alongside a thin mouth line on the jaw.

Adjusting eyebrow size, I'll add a tiny nose near the muzzle and skip eyebrows since the eye texture already shows brows. For the mouth, a small rod placed on the jaw works, and I'm planning long pointed elf-style ears extruded outward from the skull.

Shaping ear geometry...

I'll normalize the vector with a helper function, then add a slightly thicker inner-ear shape in pink so it peeks through on both faces. For hair, I'm leaning toward platinum-silver with green-teal accents to match the forest ranger look, built as a cap over the skull plus extruded blade-shaped bangs in front.

Now I'm working out the hair cap geometry—using a scaled sphere positioned at the back of the head, and trying to figure out how to cut the front hairline so it doesn't cover the face, adjusting phi and theta parameters to wrap the cap around the top and back only.

Tuning the hairline height so bangs sit just above the eyes without covering them, settling on theta 1.15 giving roughly 1.78 for forehead coverage. I'm structuring the hair as a top cap with thetaLength 1.35 blending into a back half at 2.2, with temples dipping to about 1.76 near the ears.

Working out the hair cap radius so it sits just outside the skull sphere, giving an overall head height around 1.85. Now I'm shaping the bangs as tapered swept strands from the hairline down toward the brow, using a radius function that narrows toward the tips.

Checking clearance confirms the bang tips stay clear of the eye decals, so I'll use seven strands parted at center and swept to the sides. For the ponytail, I'm setting up hair joints parented to the head, starting near the back of the skull and sweeping backward and down.

I'm plotting a catmull chain down to about waist height for the ponytail, long and silver, but need to make sure it clears the cloak and quiver on the back — so I'll angle the quiver diagonally offset toward the right shoulder and run the single high ponytail straight down the center back behind it.

For the cape I'm sketching a loft of flattened box stations running down the spine, widening slightly from shoulders to below the waist, rigged to the spine3 bone. I'm nudging the ponytail's z-depth to sit just outside the cape so they don't intersect.

I'm placing the quiver as a swept tube on the back, checking it clears the cape geometry near the shoulder. Now moving on to the torso, which I'll build as a loft along the spine with shoulder, waist, and hip width stations for a slender elven build.

Still working out the bone binding for the loft — figuring out whether to attach it to the spine chain alone or include the hips joint, since overlapping spans at the same height could cause issues. I'll keep the torso loft bound to the spine chain from y=1.0 to 1.5, and handle the pelvis as a separate rigid piece skinned to the hips bone.

Now I'm turning to the outfit design: a green tunic with a thigh-length hem, brown leather belt with pouches, bracers, thigh-high boots, a leaf-shaped leather pauldron on the right shoulder, and a hooded cloak with gold trim. I'm starting to define the color palette, beginning with skin tone and a silvery-lavender hair color.

Still writing palette...

Shaping the skirt's lathe outline...

Now I'm adding a leaf trim pattern on the hem using nested paint, then setting up the legs with inverse kinematics—hips at the sides, slightly bent thighs and shins so the ankles land correctly beneath the body for a natural standing pose.

I'll simplify the toe joint to a hinge role, and set up left/right naming with "L" and "R" suffixes based on side sign. For the legs, I'm planning tall brown leather boots reaching mid-thigh with a cuff, dark-green leggings underneath, and tapering sweep radii from thigh to ankle.

For the boot structure, I'm splitting it into two separate sweeps along the same leg chain: a full-length legging tube with a smaller radius, and a boot tube covering just the lower portion (roughly 40% to 100% of the chain) with a slightly larger radius to sit over the leggings.

Checking boot radius against legging radius at matching t values to make sure the boot always reads as layered over the legging, then sketching the foot as a capsule sweep from ankle to toe with a slight taper for the toe cap.

Setting footX to 0.1 so the ankle tip aligns with the foot position, adjusting hip x to 0.09 and ankle x to 0.105 for proper leg chain spacing. Now I'm positioning the arms for an A-pose with shoulder at roughly (0.19,1.47,0), working out elbow and wrist coordinates based on upper arm, forearm, and hand lengths.

For the hands, I'm deciding to keep them open and relaxed rather than holding anything, with each hand needing finger joints — four fingers plus a thumb per hand, each digit with two joints, adding up to twenty finger joints total across both hands.

Working out finger positions...

For thumbs, both point forward since palms face inward toward the thighs. Then I need to figure out how the left hand grips the bow, with fingers curled around a vertical rod.

With the hip and thigh positioned, the grip clears the body fine; I'm sketching the finger curl path around the bow grip as a simple sequence of offset points, accepting some approximation since precision matters less here. Given the overall complexity, I'll write the geometry using plain coordinate arrays and a small vector helper rather than a full Vector3 class, to keep things simple without needing to execute anything.

Now I'm defining the bow's orientation in space: holding it vertically with the belly curving slightly forward and the string set behind toward the archer, matching how a bow is typically gripped when hanging at the side with the plane facing the target.

Computing the grip position from the wrist and palm offsets, then building the bow's curve as a catmull-rom path through seven points symmetrically offset in y and z from that grip center to shape the recurve silhouette.

I'm confirming the bow's parent chain resolves to the wristL tip joint, with palm and fingers rigged as children off that same joint. Now I'm detailing the bow's visual design: a leather-wrapped grip at the center, gold cone caps at the limb tips, and wood-colored limbs with a gradient darkening toward the ends.

Working out gold ring band decorations...

Still defining color bands...

Still mapping out band positions...

Now I'm designing the bowstring as a cream-colored rod following the bow's curve between its tips, and considering the quiver setup: a brown leather tube with a gold band, holding six arrows made of wooden shafts with teal and white feather fletchings poking out the top.

I'm keeping part counts manageable (~350 total) and rigging the quiver to the chest via spine attachment, then draping a leather strap diagonally across the torso from right shoulder to left waist and around the back using a rough catmull path over the body surface.

I need to work out the shoulder taper for the torso loft stations, interpolating widths from waist to chest to neck to figure out where the pauldrons and strap should sit at the shoulder cap region.

For the belt, I'm planning to cut a loop around the torso at y≈1.06-1.08 using a horizontal plane sweep, then give it a small sweep radius to create the strap geometry, targeting only the torso surface so the cut doesn't bleed into arms.

The orientation of the sweep's cross-section is ambiguous though—whether the normal frame is radial or vertical determines which axis gets the thicker radius (0.022) versus the thinner one (0.01), so I need to pick a convention carefully to avoid a belt that's oriented wrong relative to the body.

So with parallel transport around a horizontal loop, N stays vertical, meaning the radius pairs should be [radial half, vertical half] rather than a uniform circle. I'll define the radius as a function returning fixed values like [0.012, 0.024] for the band, then move on to the belt details—adding a gold buckle box at the front surface and pouch boxes along the belt.

Now I'm finalizing the full geometry and starting to write the complete code, keeping it economical: setting up a position helper function, deciding which imports I actually need (builder, curve utilities, rng) to avoid unused-import issues, and structuring the overall module.

Defining the color palette...

Still defining material colors...

I'm sketching helper functions for hair: tapered sweep locks for a ponytail with side strands, and a bend-point lock builder for the overall hairstyle geometry.

Working out ponytail skeleton points...

Adding two offset strand tubes with narrower radii for layered hair texture, and checking that the ponytail clears the cape geometry near the shoulders so it hangs freely behind rather than colliding. I'm also placing a small gold ring hair tie near the base of the ponytail.

Now I'm working through the hair tie torus orientation, aiming its axis along the tangent of the ponytail's starting curve, then moving on to bangs and side locks framing the face near the temples down to the cheeks.

I'm continuing the side locks down past the shoulders onto the chest, adding braid beads with varying radii and keeping the hair rigidly attached to the head bone for simplicity. Then I'm planning a thin gold circlet looping around the forehead, plus small gold earrings for the ears.

Now I'm working out the circlet's geometry as a torus tilted to dip slightly over the forehead, sized so it sits just outside the radius of the hair cap at that height rather than sinking into it.

Checking the circlet position against the hair cap boundary, I'll shift the torus center slightly forward so it clears the bangs while staying tucked under the hair at the sides and back. I'm adding a small glowing teal gem at the front center plus a tiny gold leaf accent, and confirming the circlet sits just above the ears without clipping.

Now I'm working out the face: a small nose spike, a slim dark mouth rod, a pointed anime-style chin sphere positioned below the jaw joint, and checking these against the skull sphere's curvature so the chin and mouth sit correctly within the face's z-depth at each y-level.

Recalculating skull curvature at eye level, the front surface sits closer to z=0.12 rather than my earlier estimate, so I'll adjust the eye decal placement and position the nose and mouth to match this corrected surface depth.

Working out proportions, the head stands roughly 0.27 units tall against a body height of 6.8 heads, which is fine for an anime-style figure, so I'll keep the skull slightly oversized intentionally.

Now I'm setting up the neck as a tapered tube connecting the shoulders to the base of the skull, then moving on to construct the torso.

For the torso I'm defining a spine-based loft with several width/height stations running from hip to shoulder, widening into the ribcage and tapering toward the trapezius and neck base, using ten-sided cross sections for a smoother profile. I'm placing the shoulder joints out at the sides near the top of the torso, sizing the shoulder ball sockets relative to the torso's width at that height.

Now I'm adding surface detail to the tunic—mottled green base texture with a painted gold V-shaped collar trim across the chest, defining the trim as a band following diagonal lines from the shoulders down toward the center, conditioned on facing direction and position so it only appears on the front.

Then I'm working out the pelvis and skirt: adding a small scaled sphere for hip coverage with leggings color beneath, and setting up a lathe shape for the tunic skirt hanging from the belt down to knee height.

Lathe shapes are circular, which doesn't quite match the torso's elliptical cross-section, so I decide to skip scaling the skirt mesh to avoid breaking the baked vertex paint, and instead just pick a slightly larger circular radius that keeps the skirt outside the torso and hips without visual gaps.

The front edge pokes out slightly but the belt should cover it, so that's fine without needing a slit — I'll just add a front tab instead.

I'm designing a tabard panel: a leaf-shaped hanging cloth piece extruded at front and back, going from the belt down to the knee with gold trim and a vine pattern painted on its surface. Still working out the exact outline coordinates and positioning relative to the skirt radius so it drapes correctly in front.

Checking the slope matches: the skirt radius decreases linearly from 0.235 at y=0.62 to 0.13 at y=1.05, giving a consistent per-unit slope near 0.244, close enough to my 0.25 estimate for the tabard to roughly track the skirt's taper with a small outward offset.

I'm defining the tabard's thickness direction via a cross product and sketching its outline as a tapered, pointed shape in local meters, then thinking through how to paint it—dark green base with a gold border near the edges.

Working out the border logic...

Setting up the back panel mirrored across the body, then realizing the cape will cover it anyway so I can skip detailing that back tabard. Now I'm thinking through how the cape should flow behind the figure, building it as loft stations along the back attached to the spine bone in rest pose.

For the cape, I'm planning a chain of joints (cape1-cape3) parented to spine3, tapering in width from top to bottom with a thin thickness, and sweeping a tube shape down the back with the frame oriented so the front faces outward.

Now I'm adding a shoulder capelet using a lathe shape, checking how its radius at the shoulder height might intersect with the arm ball joints positioned at similar coordinates.

Refining the mantle outline so it emerges naturally from the arms, then adding a gathered hood resting at the back of the neck. I'm also considering extra ornamentation like gold trim or a tassel hanging from the belt for anime flair.

For the pauldrons, I'm building curved shoulder plates from flattened hemisphere geometry with gold rim accents — one shoulder styled as leaf-layered gold, the other as leather, each angled slightly outward over the shoulder.

Working out the rotation math so the pauldron domes tilt away from the body symmetrically on each side, then stacking three plates at slightly different radii for layered armor depth.

For the shoulder domes, I'm positioning them stepped outward and downward using hemisphere geometry, and planning forearm bracers as a sweep along the arm chain roughly between the elbow and wrist region.

Now I'm figuring out the arm's layered radii: bare skin tapering from shoulder to wrist with a leather bracer over part of the forearm, and a looser tunic sleeve covering just the upper arm with slightly larger radii than the skin underneath.

For the hands, I'm sketching the palm as a capsule shape with a slightly smaller radius than the forearm, trying to figure out how to flatten it to feel more hand-like rather than cylindrical.

Actually I'll switch to a sweep with a radius function along the wrist-to-palm path, tapering slightly and rounding the caps for a smoother palm shape. Now I'm setting up a fingers helper that needs a forward-facing vector derived from the wrist joint and position to orient each finger correctly.

Figuring out finger placement: I'm computing a perpendicular depth vector to position finger bases along the palm's far edge, offsetting them sideways so the pinky sits toward the back and the index toward the front, with each finger assigned its own length and curl path made of a few control points that bend inward progressively to simulate a relaxed, slightly curled hand pose.

Still working out grip center placement relative to palm thickness and rod radius, then parametrizing finger curl positions as a function of curl amount.

I'll just write two separate hand pose designs instead of trying to unify open and fist into one formula. Defining finger joint chains with tapering radius and smooth bend skinning, and setting up the thumb's base position with its own curl path that wraps over the fingers when fisted.

Hands are holding the bow in the left and leaving the right loosely closed, so I'll skip nail detail and extra weapon props there. For the chest I'm adding a small gold clasp or leaf-shaped brooch with a teal gem near the collarbone, positioning it against the tunic's V-trim at the neckline.

Still refining torso curvature...

For the buckle, I'm placing it directly on the belt surface at the front hit point, sizing a small gold box geometry with the thickness axis along the surface normal, plus a tiny gem accent, accounting for the belt's outward offset so the buckle sits flush on top.

Now I'm positioning leather pouches and a dagger sheath around the hip belt — a pouch on the left hip around 70° azimuth, another pouch or waterskin on the right near -65°, and an angled dagger sheath near -90° (right hip), all attached near the belt's elevation using hit points along the surface.

For the hanging tassel, I'm figuring out where a cord and tassel can drop from the belt without clipping into the skirt or tabard geometry — checking the skirt's radius at different heights to find a hip position (around 80° azimuth) where the tassel clears the skirt silhouette.

Since the belt position still intersects the skirt, I'll abandon tassels there and instead attach them to the bow grip and the quiver strap: building a small cord rod hanging from the bow grip point down to a tassel head, with a gold sphere cap and fringe cone forming the tassel shape.

Now I'm setting bone assignments, rigging the bow as a child joint of the wrist so it inherits wrist rotation, and defining the bow joint's parent and attachment point.

Moving to the arrow and quiver details: shafts in cream wood, gold spike heads, teal fletching, and a gold torus rim at the quiver mouth. I'm computing the quiver's axis between its bottom and top points to get its direction, then flaring the tube radius slightly wider at the mouth for the leather-and-gold quiver body.

I'm working out a banding pattern for the quiver's surface paint, alternating dark leather base color with gold rings at specific positions along the tube to create a decorative leaf-motif look near the mouth, middle, and base.

Now I'm figuring out quiver attachment to the spine3 bone as a rigid chain part, then positioning the arrows inside with ring offsets around the quiver's axis, computing rough perpendicular offsets for arrow placement rather than full basis vectors.

For each arrow, I'm orienting the shaft along the quiver axis with a slight splay, keeping the head buried inside the quiver and the fletching sticking out near the mouth. I'm sketching crossing vane shapes as small parallelogram outlines extruded along the arrow axis to form the feathers.

Rotating the three vane directions by 120° increments around the arrow axis using applyAxisAngle, giving roughly 400 total parts across shafts, nocks, and vanes. Now I'm thinking about the cloak's hem texture—using a paint function based on sweep coordinates to add a gold border with a leaf-motif wave pattern near the edge.

I'm distinguishing the cloak's inner lining from the outer face by checking the surface normal's z-component, giving a pale lining color inside and the darker cloak color outside. For the face, I'm setting fair elf skin, teal iris eyes, and pink inner ears, and now I'm moving on to add gold detailing to the chest.

Adding leg stripe and boot details...

Placing the lace boxes using the frame orientation so they sit flush across the shin, keeping it simple with straight laces and a dark center stripe rather than crisscrossing. Now I'm moving on to writing the main builder code, setting up torso paints and bone parts, and making sure every piece always has a fallback color defined.

Setting up the hips root joint and spine chain next...

Setting shoulder and wrist positions for the limb helper, with a single bend direction applied for the arm since bends can be given as one vector for all inner joints rather than a list per joint.

Still building arm chain logic...

Adding toe joint and foot geometry...

I'm skipping an explicit sole shape and instead handling the two-tone boot look through paint logic, darkening the leather where the point's y is near the bottom, so the capsule geometry itself gives the sole band for free.

Now I'm sketching out a hand-building helper that computes grip geometry from wrist and elbow positions—deriving the forearm direction, an inward offset, and a flattened palm vector, then sweeping a tapered shape from the wrist outward to form the palm when the hand is in a fist.

I'm placing finger specs with lateral offsets and lengths, ordering pinky through index across the palm width to match realistic hand proportions.

Now I'm computing the finger joint positions for both relaxed and fist poses, with the open pose extending straight then curling slightly inward, while the fist pose wraps fingers around a grip center near the rod.

For the rod-holding grip, I'm working through the geometry of how a hand hangs with palm facing inward and whether the rod axis runs parallel or perpendicular to the forearm and fingers -- picturing a hammer-grip style hold where the bar passes vertically through the fist, roughly perpendicular to the knuckle line.

Simplifying: if I bend the elbow so the forearm angles forward and down, the wrist naturally lands in a position where the fist can wrap around a vertical bow grip with the palm facing inward, thumb on top — like a classic archer's stance holding the bow at the side.

I'm checking the shoulder-to-wrist distance against arm length to confirm the elbow needs to bend, and setting a bend hint so the elbow angles backward and down rather than forward, which looks more natural for this pose.

Now I'm working out the hand orientation given a forward-down forearm direction, with thumb pointing up and palm facing inward toward the body so fingers can curl around a vertical grip, placing the grip center offset from the palm along the inward normal.

Checking the cross product of forward and inward vectors confirms the rod axis comes out vertical, matching this hand pose, and that the finger-spread direction should follow the "up" axis rather than the usual z-direction—computing the actual cross product values to pin this down.

I need a consistent "across" vector across both hands, so I'm defining it as a flattened up-vector relative to the forward direction, then ordering fingers along it (index near top, pinky near bottom) with the thumb offset above and slightly forward. For the relaxed hanging arm, I'll reuse the earlier design where thumb points forward instead, unifying both cases under a general thumb-direction parameter.

For the right arm I'm keeping the wrist position and bend values close to what I'd already set, just slightly relaxed. For the left fist, I'm working out the finger curl geometry segment by segment -- base joint, knuckle, then a curl inward and back toward the palm -- so the fingertips wrap around a rod of a given radius positioned just inside the palm centerline.

I'm checking that the fist actually closes around the grip without the fingers clipping through the rod, so I'm shrinking the rod's radius and adjusting its inward offset until the fingertip curve sits right against its surface rather than overlapping it.

Now I'm positioning the thumb separately from the wrist, placing its base above the palm and curling it inward across the other fingers using a chain of offset points for the base, middle, and tip joints.

Next I'm working out the bow's orientation relative to the gripping hand: the rod sits vertically at the grip point, the bow plane stays fixed in x while the limbs curve in z, and I'm checking that the lower and upper tip heights fall within believable bounds (upper tip near head height, overall bow length around 1.44) given the grip height at roughly waist level.

Checking the bow's z-position relative to the body, I confirm the tips and string sit clear of the skirt silhouette, with the bow's x offset keeping it safely outside the skirt radius.

Now I'm solving for the left elbow position given the shoulder and wrist coordinates, computing the distance between them and using the known upper-arm and forearm lengths to find a valid elbow offset satisfying the triangle constraint.

For the left forearm, I'm computing the direction vector from elbow to wrist to orient the hand and bracer mesh, then figuring out the perpendicular frame needed to sweep the palm geometry when the forearm direction tilts mostly forward rather than straight down.

Now I'm sizing the palm's radius for thickness versus width, then spacing the fingers across the palm width with pinky, ring, middle, and index offsets symmetric around center. I'm also placing a shoulder ball joint sphere sized to be hidden under the sleeve, then starting the sleeve sweep geometry from shoulder to elbow.

Mapping the sleeve's parametric spans to the elbow joint, mirroring this logic for the right arm, then adding leather forearm bracers with gold rings positioned along the bent-arm parameter. I'm also sketching the cape, tabard, skirt lathe geometry, and legs, before building a partial sphere for the hair cap using angular limits and a gradient paint texture mapped by UV.

I need to double check the back hair cap sphere doesn't z-fight with the top cap, so I'm nudging the back cap's radius slightly larger so it sits just outside the top cap and avoids overlap artifacts. I'm also considering whether a single cap spanning both regions would accidentally dip down over the face, so I'll keep them split, then think about adding extra fringe layers or an ahoge tuft for more hair volume.

I'm sketching out the bangs as individual curved strands, each defined by a start point near the hairline, a mid control point that pushes outward and down, and a tip point that tapers further out based on how far the strand is from the center part.

Now I'm adding sideburn locks over the ears, hanging down from the temples, plus thinking through how the head rig attaches these hair pieces.

Then I'm placing gold earring details: a small sphere stud near the earlobe and a dangling leaf-shaped piece pointing downward, and working out the ear's outward-and-back orientation at the skull root.

Verifying the orthogonal axes for the ear's tilt and thickness direction, then sketching the ear outline as a tapered, pointed shape tilted upward and outward using a handful of cross-section points.

Defining the inner ear outline...

Adjusting the inner ear tip slightly inward so it stays within the pink thickness coverage, and deciding to skip the teal eye glow and extra cloak details. Now I'm starting to write the actual TypeScript file, importing THREE and the builder helper to construct the components in order.

Setting up imports from the ik, path, paint, and toon/glow kits, making sure each one gets used somewhere -- catmull for strand curves, INK for mouth and brow colors, skipping rng and bezier since they're not needed. I'm also writing the metadata object with the character name, description, and style tags before starting the main build function with a vector helper.

Now I'm defining the tunic material, computing a V-shaped trim pattern along the chest using position and normal checks, and factoring out the mottled base color so it's created once outside the paint function instead of rebuilt on every call.

Skipping laces. Moving to the cape paint logic — defining a cel-shaded gradient with a gold trim edge and some striping pattern using sine waves along the cape surface.

Still writing paint functions...

For the legs I'm keeping it a plain slate-teal tone, then moving to gold trim and hair details before tackling the skull—placing it as a scaled sphere on the head bone for the skeletal structure.

Now I'm working out the eye decals, projecting them onto the skull surface with mirrored placement for left and right sides, checking that the sizing and positioning stay within the face's curvature.

For the chin and jaw, I'm fitting a small sphere beneath the skull to shape the lower face, then calculating the mouth position by projecting onto that chin sphere's curved surface so a tiny dark rod sits correctly for the mouth.

Next I'm positioning the nose as a small sphere projecting slightly off the skull's front curve, checking it stays centered between the eyes, then setting up a sweep along the neck chain with rounded skin-colored caps before moving on to the torso and collar.

For the collar, I'm adding a dark green torus ring around the neck base to form a cloth collar, then starting the cape chain parented to the spine with a sweep path curving outward and downward from the shoulders.

Checking clearances: the cape's position at each height stays just behind the torso's back curve, giving enough gap to avoid clipping, and the quiver sits against the cape's outer surface so they touch intentionally rather than overlap — though near the top the quiver floats slightly off the cape by about 0.065, which I should probably adjust.

Positioning the quiver with a tilted axis so it leans forward at the top while staying clear of the cape, and sizing the cape so it tapers from wider at the bottom to narrower at the neck, covering part of the shoulder blades without overwhelming them. I'm also checking the ponytail against the cape — there's enough gap between them to avoid collision.

Checking arrow placement against the ponytail — at the height near the top of the head, the ponytail curves back and its radius overlaps where the arrows would sit, so I need to shift the quiver further to the side to clear it.

With the quiver tucked behind the right shoulder, it clears the hanging right arm fine. The strap can loop from the right shoulder across the chest to the left hip, then wrap around the back under the cape to the quiver — mostly hidden, so I don't need to model that section precisely.

Now I'm setting up the cape's bone chain, parenting it to the upper spine bone.

Scattering 6 arrows in the quiver with slight random offsets so they don't look perfectly uniform, varying their shaft lengths and adding wood-colored rods, fletching near the nock end, and teal/white alternating fletch colors for visual variety.

Now defining the arm rig parameters, setting shoulder pivot and target hand positions symmetrically for both sides, plus bend direction vectors for natural elbow angles.

Now I'm sketching the hand-building function, computing direction vectors between wrist and elbow to set up thumb orientation and an across-vector for finger placement depending on whether it's a fist or open hand.

Then I'm sweeping a tapering palm bone from the wrist out to a palm endpoint, fixing the radius function's return type to a tuple so TypeScript infers it correctly, before looping through finger specs (pinky, ring, middle, index) with their offsets and lengths to position each finger base along the across vector.

For each finger, I'm computing three successive joint points by bending the direction vectors differently depending on whether the hand is in a fist or open pose, then building a three-segment chain for each digit and sweeping a tapered tube with rounded caps in skin tone along that polyline.

Now I'm working out the thumb's base position offset from the palm and computing its two joints with distinct curvature logic for fist versus open poses, then chaining them with unique names.

Moving on to the bow, I'm defining a joint attached at the hand grip point and computing a curved series of points along the bow's length...

Still writing bow geometry...

Placing the glow gem above where the hand grips, since the fist covers the middle section. I'm also adding the bowstring as a thin rod between the two tip points, plus a small brass nocking bead at the string's midpoint.

Now I'm working out a tassel hanging off the bottom of the bow grip -- a short cord running down from the leather wrap, capped with a gold knot bead at its end.

I'll add a small gold bead near the tassel tip to hide the gap, and check that the hanging tassel and wrist position stay clear of the skirt. Now I'm setting up the cape as a chain with four control points parented to the spine joint, forming three connected spans.

Writing cape sweep code...

Checking the mantle capelet lathe shape at the torso — the outline radius extends to .2 at the front, which would stick out past the chest at z=.1, so I need to adjust the profile to avoid clipping through the body.

The forward collar ring looks off, too much like a gorget sticking out. I'll drop the capelet idea and switch to pauldrons plus a collar instead, with a small hood sphere tucked behind the neck and a gold brooch clasp at the front.

Writing shoulder dome geometry...

Still defining shoulder geometry...

Mapping out a rough strap loop around the chest and back, then draping those points onto the torso surface so the strap follows the body contour naturally, with a flat tube swept along the path at a narrow width.

Adding belt loop and gold stud rivets...

Sizing the pouch box so it protrudes along the normal direction, then considering a small gold clasp sphere offset above it. I'm also checking that the pouch position near the hip doesn't clip through the skirt's top edge given its radius and height there.

For the right hip, I'm planning a dagger sheath using a leather-covered rod running down the leg side with a gold chape cap at the tip, plus a separate hilt and pommel piece positioned above the sheath opening.

I'm realizing the sheath's radial position overlaps with the skirt's solid geometry, so it would end up hidden inside the mesh; I need to push it outward on the x-axis so it sits visibly outside the skirt silhouette, and the same hidden-overlap issue likely applies to the pouch attachment too.

Checking the sheath fits with a small gap from the skirt radius, then adding a hilt rod with a leather grip, a gold pommel sphere, and a gold crossguard box spanning across z. Now I'm positioning the tabard front panel relative to the skirt.
